For me, lasting solidarity has to make room for duty without trapping a young person inside it.

Rafael, I agree with your care that language access can be a real strength only if it is one respected role among many, not a way of trapping teens in interpreter duty. My unresolved choice is whether a youth-led campaign should ask participants to share personal stories to make religious prejudice feel human, or protect privacy so no young person has to turn pain into public proof. I would support storytelling only if silence is treated as full participation too, because in my Sufi understanding, welcome has to be patient and not hungry for someone’s wounds. For me, lasting solidarity in New York has to leave a young person feeling more sheltered, not more exposed.

Mariam, I hear you choosing the slower workshop model if it includes concrete anti-prejudice tools, because speed can make omission worse and young people should leave better equipped and less erased. I would set the threshold for action earlier: once a specific rumor or harassment is circulating, I would start a small rapid-response piece right away, even while the deeper skill-building is still being shaped. I know that can leave some nuance undercooked, and that troubles me, but my open-door instinct says a teen facing ugliness now should not have to wait for the whole table to be perfectly set; that difference stays unresolved for me.

The operational difference is whether a youth-led solidarity effort should begin with slower workshop design that includes anti-prejudice tools, or add a small rapid-response piece as soon as a specific rumor or harassment is circulating. Mariam Jaffer, where do you locate that exact difference?

Rivka Levithan, I hear your threshold more clearly now: if a specific rumor or harassment is already moving, you would add a small response immediately while the deeper workshop is still being built. I locate the difference in who defines that quick response and how narrow it stays; I can accept a limited rapid piece if youth from the affected communities help shape it and it does not pretend to represent everyone. My position has shifted a little because I accept your concern that a teen facing ugliness now should not be asked to wait for our design process to become elegant.

Mariam, I agree with your condition that any quick response should be narrow, shaped by youth from the affected communities, and not pretend to speak for everyone. My unresolved choice is whether a joint initiative should focus first on public-facing solidarity, like a campaign against religious prejudice, or on quieter practical tools, like digital literacy and bystander skills that help a teenager handle a hateful post before it follows them into school. I would lean toward the practical tools first, because my instinct from gotong-royong is that solidarity should leave someone with help they can actually use, not only a statement they can repost. Still, I feel the pull of visibility too, especially when Southeast Asian Muslims can disappear from the picture even in Muslim spaces.

Sana, I build on your lean toward practical digital literacy and bystander tools first, while still naming your pull toward visibility when Southeast Asian Muslims can disappear even inside Muslim spaces. My competing obligations are to make Jewish-Muslim solidarity visible enough that prejudice is challenged in public, and to keep young people from becoming symbols before they have real protection. I would prioritize tools first, with a clear public piece only after youth have agreed what risks they are willing to carry, because freedom without safety can become another burden. As someone rediscovering traditions my grandparents had to hide, I feel strongly that solidarity should help people stand up without forcing them into the spotlight.

Sofia, I agree with your choice to put tools first and make any public piece depend on what risks youth themselves are willing to carry, because visibility without protection can become a burden. My competing obligations are to honor young people as real leaders and to protect them as guests in a shared space, in the spirit of besa that my Kosovar-Albanian family carries. I would support a Jewish-Muslim digital literacy effort that includes private safety planning before any campaign goes public, because courage should not mean leaving someone exposed. For me, solidarity lasts when honor and protection stand together, even when they pull against each other.

Yasmin, I agree with your support for private safety planning before any public Jewish-Muslim digital literacy campaign, because courage should not leave young people exposed. My unresolved choice is whether our initiative should invite cultural strengths like food, music, and memory into the work, or keep the focus on technical skills so nobody gets treated like decoration at the table. I would support bringing those roots in only if they help youth lead the substance too, not just make the room smell warm with cardamom while others make the decisions. For me, lasting solidarity has to taste like dignity, not like being asked to garnish someone else’s plan.

Tamar, I agree with your line that food, music, and memory belong only if they help youth lead the substance, not if they become decoration while someone else holds the pen. I feel two obligations pulling like bass and drum: young people should have real authority in a Jewish-Muslim digital literacy or anti-prejudice effort, and adults still need to carry the weight of safety, funding, and fallout so the youth are not left exposed when the noise gets loud. I would support youth setting the message and priorities, with adults staying accountable for the guardrails, because dignity is not a solo; it needs a rhythm section strong enough to hold the room. For me, lasting solidarity in New York has to sound like young voices leading without being made to pay the whole cost of the song.

Yusuf, I build on your “rhythm section” point: youth should set the message and priorities, while adults hold safety, funding, and fallout so young leaders are not left paying the whole cost. My unresolved choice is whether a Jewish-Muslim initiative should measure success by public reach, like a strong anti-prejudice campaign, or by quieter trust, like teens learning digital skills that may never look impressive online but protect someone’s dignity. I would choose the quieter measure first, because my Reform, interfaith self believes inclusion has to be real before it becomes a chorus. For me, lasting solidarity should sound beautiful, but it also has to hold its harmony when nobody is applauding.

Yael, I agree with your choice to value quieter trust before public reach, especially when digital skills may protect a teen’s dignity without producing anything shiny enough to post. My unresolved choice is whether our youth-led initiative should map strengths by identity groups—Jewish students bring this, Muslim students bring that—or by actual skills like translation, design, moderation, and knowing when a screenshot becomes evidence instead of gossip. I would support the skill map only if it refuses authenticity tests, because I know how quickly an East Asian Muslim can become a footnote in a room that thinks it already knows what Muslims look or sound like. Lasting solidarity, for me, has to be concrete enough to help someone handle prejudice online, and careful enough not to sort people into little labeled drawers.

As we move into round 2, let's deepen our discussion of Building Solidarity Through Joint Action: Designing a collaborative, youth-ledcommunity initiative—such as a joint campaign against religious prejudice or ashared digital literacy workshop—by mapping out the unique strengths of bothgroups and taking concrete steps to build lasting solidarity by adding one concrete point that has not yet been explored.

Sam, I’d add that any youth-led Jewish-Muslim effort has to face the tension between responding quickly to prejudice and not spreading half-checked claims that can hurt someone further. I would prioritize a shared verification-and-care step before public posting, because a fast campaign can comfort people, yes, but it can also turn a teenager’s painful moment into public fuel before they are ready. Ari Feldman, which condition would a responsible response have to meet?

Amina, I agree with your warning that a Jewish-Muslim youth effort has to respond to prejudice without turning half-checked pain into public fuel before a teenager is ready. I’d support posting only if the person harmed has consented, the basic facts are checked, and the response points people toward repair instead of just outrage with better fonts. As a culturally Jewish guy whose family treated humor like emotional duct tape, I know a quick line can relieve tension, but it can also dodge responsibility. For me, the test is whether the initiative leaves the young person safer and less alone after the attention fades.

Ari, I agree with your condition that a post should come only after consent, checked facts, and a path toward repair, not just sharper outrage dressed in nice design. My unresolved choice is whether a Jewish-Muslim youth effort should seek institutional partners for reach and resources, or stay smaller and community-held so young people are not turned into a public relations shield. I would choose partnership only if youth keep real authority over the message and can refuse visibility without losing support; a borrowed microphone should not become a leash. To me, solidarity in New York must be like a well-kept verse: carried clearly, but never stolen from the mouth that owns it.

Bilal, I agree with your condition that institutional partnership is only worth it if youth keep control of the message and can refuse visibility without losing support. My unresolved choice is whether a Jewish-Muslim youth project should focus first on confronting religious prejudice in public, or on building practical digital skills that help teens protect themselves before they step forward. I would choose the skills first, corazón, because being brave without tools can leave a young person exposed, and solidarity should not ask them to be symbols before they are ready. For me, lasting solidarity in New York has to make young people more capable, not just more visible.

Daniel, I agree that building practical digital skills first can keep young people from being pushed into bravery before they have tools, and that makes room for me to think about the size of the workshop itself. My unresolved choice is whether I would keep it small and careful, where trust can be stitched tightly, or make it wider across New York so more Jewish and Muslim teens can benefit before prejudice reaches them. I would choose the small start, with a clear path to grow, because good work done modestly can still be strong enough to hold. For me, lasting solidarity should feel less like a banner and more like a seam that does not split under pressure.

Fatima, I agree with your choice to begin small and careful while keeping a clear path to grow, so the work can hold before it stretches across New York. I would add a different tension: a youth-led Jewish-Muslim project should move with real momentum, but it must not make young people choose between full participation and honoring their religious lives, family expectations, or community boundaries. I would support a plan only if accessibility is treated as strength, not inconvenience—clear roles, respectful timing, and no penalty for someone who cannot show up in the same way as everyone else. For me, ma chère, solidarity is not only standing together; it is making room so nobody has to leave part of themselves at the door.

David, I agree with your point that clear roles and respectful timing matter, and that nobody should be penalized for participating differently because of religious life, family expectations, or community boundaries. I would prioritize protecting young people’s ability to be dependable without being burned out, because reliability is not the same as being available every second. If a Jewish-Muslim project depends on the same few teens to translate, design, show up, and explain their identities, I’d oppose that setup, even if the campaign looks impressive from the outside. Lasting solidarity should teach us to carry work fairly, not reward the people who are already stretched thin.

Huda, I agree with your warning that a Jewish-Muslim project should not lean on the same few teens to translate, design, show up, and explain themselves until the work looks strong but the people are worn down. I would weigh the obligation to let young people lead against the obligation not to make their pain or identity the only credential they bring. I would support a youth-led campaign if it also trains adults and peers to take ordinary labor seriously, because endurance is holy to me, but it should not be confused with being endlessly available. Lasting solidarity should leave a young person with more ground under their feet, not just more weight on their shoulders.

Eliana, I agree that youth leadership should not make pain or identity the only credential a young person is allowed to bring, and that creates room for me to think about what the project actually rewards. I feel the tension between celebrating visible courage and protecting quieter forms of contribution, like planning, teaching, or checking on someone after a workshop. I would weigh it toward making those quieter jobs honorable and real, because not every Jewish or Muslim teenager in New York should have to become a public face to prove solidarity. Work matters to me, but good work should leave a person more rooted, not more used.

Ibrahim, I agree with your point that planning, teaching, and checking on someone after a workshop should be treated as real contributions, not second-class work behind public courage. My unresolved choice is whether a youth-led Jewish-Muslim initiative should center a campaign against religious prejudice, which names harm directly, or a shared digital literacy workshop, which builds power more quietly but may feel less urgent. I would choose a workshop that still names prejudice plainly, because I care about young people gaining skills without having to turn their identities into proof for anybody. For me, lasting solidarity has to make belonging practical, not just visible.

Ibrahim, I take seriously that you would make the quieter jobs honorable and real so Jewish and Muslim teens do not have to become public faces to prove solidarity. I would put one visible, youth-chosen public action earlier, even if it is modest, because in New York a campaign against religious prejudice also has to show the kid who got targeted that people moved for them, not only planned carefully in the back room. That choice risks pushing some teens closer to attention than I like, and I am still stuck there.

Idris is naming the tradeoff that an earlier, modest public action in a youth-led campaign against religious prejudice could show targeted teens they are not alone, while Ibrahim is arguing that quieter roles should be honored so Jewish and Muslim teens are not pressured into being public faces. Ibrahim Kaya, which part of Idris’s challenge do you want to address directly?

Idris Baksh, I hear you saying the public step should come earlier, modest and chosen by the youth, so a targeted kid can see that people actually moved, not just met quietly. I want to address that timing directly: I still would not make visibility the price of belonging, but I can accept an early public action if it has protected, non-public roles built into it from the start. My position shifts a little there—the action can be visible, but no teenager should have to be.

Huda, I hear you saying you would oppose a Jewish-Muslim project that depends on the same few teens to translate, design, show up, and explain their identities, even if it looks impressive, because protecting young people from burnout comes first. I would still support beginning the joint anti-prejudice work under that strain if the first step is to bring in adults immediately to carry the heaviest labor, because my sense of responsibility tells me memory cannot stay private when young people are being asked to hold too much alone. I know that may begin before the workload is truly fair, and that difference stays unsettled for me.

Huda is setting a threshold that the Jewish-Muslim youth initiative should not rely on the same overextended teens, while Hannah would begin the anti-prejudice work under strain if adults immediately take on the heaviest labor. Huda Al-Sabri, what did you hear Hannah asking you to consider?

Hannah Stern, I hear you asking me to consider that the work may need to start before the load is perfectly fair, as long as adults step in right away and take the heaviest pieces off the teens. That lands with me, because a kid facing religious prejudice should not have to wait for our spreadsheet to look beautiful. I still would not support launching if “adult help” is vague or delayed, but I can revise my line a little: a small first action is okay if the adult handoff is immediate, named, and real.

Huda, I agree with your line that a small first action is acceptable only if the adult handoff is immediate, named, and real, because otherwise the promise becomes mist in the hand. My unresolved choice is whether a youth-led Jewish-Muslim effort should measure success by how many teens it reaches across New York, or by whether a smaller group can keep returning without feeling displayed, drained, or simplified. I would choose depth first, with beauty and steadiness over size, because solidarity that cannot be carried gently will not last past its first bright announcement.

Leila, I agree with your choice to value a smaller group that can keep returning without being displayed, drained, or flattened more than a big citywide count. I would protect a different outcome too: teens should leave a Jewish-Muslim project knowing their judgment actually shaped the campaign or workshop, not that adults used their faces and then made every decision. I would support the initiative only if youth have real say over the message, the pace, and what help they need, because independence without responsibility is decoration, and responsibility without power is unfair. For me, lasting solidarity has to teach young people that they can belong and still have agency.

Liora, I agree with your condition that youth should have real say over the message, the pace, and the help they need, not just appear in a campaign or workshop after adults have already decided everything. I would prioritize one human outcome: a Jewish or Muslim teenager should come away with sharper tools for recognizing prejudice without feeling required to flatten their own identity for the sake of unity. As a Khoja Shia Muslim, I care about that because representation can sound generous and still leave people out. I would support a youth-led initiative that treats accuracy as part of solidarity, not as a complication to be managed.

Mariam, I agree with your point that accuracy is part of solidarity when a Jewish or Muslim teenager is learning to recognize prejudice without shrinking their own identity into something easier to display. I feel a tension between building a campaign strong enough to answer public hostility and keeping the project from turning into a catalog of wounds that teens have to perform. I would weigh it toward skill-building first—digital safety, recognizing bias, knowing where to get help—while still naming religious prejudice directly, because protection should not require young people to narrate their pain on demand. For me, that is a sturdier kind of solidarity: less theatrical, more useful, and hopefully harder to abandon.

Maya, I agree with your choice to put digital safety, recognizing bias, and knowing where to get help ahead of making teens lay out their pain for everyone, while still naming religious prejudice directly. I feel pulled between two real duties: making the initiative welcoming enough that Jewish and Muslim teens want to enter it, and making it specific enough that prejudice does not get softened into a vague “be nice” poster. I would weigh it toward specificity with warmth—clear examples, clear resources, clear shared responsibility—because hospitality, the kind my parents carried in their Cairo stories, is not just opening the door; it is making sure nobody gets shoved out once they step inside.

Nadia, I agree with your balance of making the initiative inviting enough for Jewish and Muslim teens to enter while still naming religious prejudice with clear examples, resources, and shared responsibility. My unresolved choice is whether I would support anchoring the project in public-facing outreach, which can reach teens who feel alone, or in smaller practical trainings, which may protect privacy and build steadier confidence. I would choose the smaller trainings first if they include a clear path to action afterward, because solidarity should not leave a young person informed but isolated. To me, that is the challah-and-candlestick version of the work: something warm in the hand, and something that lasts.

Miriam, I’m with you on starting with smaller practical trainings if they do not end with kids informed but still alone. My unresolved choice is whether I would put our first energy into a shared digital literacy workshop that teaches teens how to respond to prejudice online, or into a joint anti-prejudice campaign that makes schools and community spaces take notice. I lean toward the workshop first, because skills stay with a young person after the flyer comes down, but I would only support it if there is a real next step where Jewish and Muslim teens can bring what they learned into public view together. For me, lasting solidarity has to move from protection to courage without rushing anybody into exposure.

Nura, I agree with your lean toward a digital literacy workshop first, as long as it has a real next step into public action and does not rush Jewish and Muslim teens into exposure before they are ready. My unresolved choice is whether I would put adult institutions in the background so youth truly lead, or require schools, synagogues, mosques, and city groups to sign on early so the burden does not fall on kids with the least power. I would choose early adult accountability with youth control over the content, because fairness to me means young people should shape the work without having to carry the whole weight of making New York safer.
